findings.title: enableSqlExpressions function is confusingly written and could be misread as respecting the feature flag
findings.body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false (disabling the feature) but is written with a misleading `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` computation and two `return false` branches that suggest the flag matters when it does not. The parameter `h` is also taken but only its `features` field is consulted in a dead computation. A future maintainer trying to 'restore' the feature is likely to flip the function back to `return !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)` (matching the variable naming) and reintroduce CVE-2024-9264, because the current logic gives no indication that the hard-coded `false` is deliberate. The function should be reduced to a single `return false` with a clear comment, or the call site should be inlined and the function removed.

findings.title: Error message implies SQL expressions may be implemented later
findings.body: When SQL expressions are disabled, the code returns `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message suggests the feature is a work in progress that may be completed later, which conflicts with the security-driven intent of this PR to keep the feature disabled. A user-facing message such as "SQL expressions are disabled" would more accurately convey the state and avoid confusing operators who read the error in logs.

findings.title: TablesList still concatenates rawSQL into a DuckDB command but is now only safe by accident
findings.body: `TablesList` still builds `cmd := fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` from user-controlled `rawSQL` (with only a naive single-quote doubling) and passes it to `RunCommands`. The current fix only neutralises this because `RunCommands` is now a stub returning an error. If the stub is ever removed or replaced to re-enable SQL expressions, this exact code path is the one that was exploited (CVE-2024-9264): the rawSQL is interpolated into a shell-style command string passed to DuckDB. The function should either be deleted outright, or hardened (e.g. reject input containing anything other than an allow-listed SQL skeleton) so that the vulnerability cannot reappear by simply swapping the stub back.

findings.title: No automated test added for the SQL-expressions disabled behaviour
findings.body: This is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that hard-codes SQL expressions to be disabled. The PR description only mentions manual testing by the author and a Slack confirmation; no automated regression test was added. A unit test in `pkg/expr` that calls `ReadQuery` (or `UnmarshalSQLCommand`) with a `QueryTypeSQL` payload and asserts the resulting error is the only thing preventing the vulnerability from being silently re-enabled in a future refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or removal of the stub in `pkg/expr/sql/db.go`.

findings.title: UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs an executable SQLCommand and is not covered by the reader-level disable
findings.body: The PR only gates SQL expressions inside `ReadQuery` in `pkg/expr/reader.go`. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` is a separate code path that calls `NewSQLCommand` directly, which in turn calls `sql.TablesList`. The function is only safe today because `sql.NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands`/`QueryFramesInto` are stubs returning errors. Any future caller of `UnmarshalSQLCommand` (e.g. another endpoint or a test harness that bypasses the reader) would not be stopped by the `enableSqlExpressions` check. The disable should be enforced at the shared `NewSQLCommand` entry point (returning the same error) so both code paths are covered by a single guard, not just the reader.
